conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m really glad you’re here. My job is to support new mothers’ emotional well-being, and a routine part of that support is a quick check-in called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a simple, 10-question screen that helps us see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger, so please answer as openly as feels safe. We’ll go question by question, and it usually takes just a few minutes. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly... not much. I’ve laughed maybe once or twice when my husband made a silly joke, but even then it felt kind of forced. Most of the time I just feel too tired or down to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly just here and there—like once or twice when my husband cracked a joke—but even then the laugh felt kind of hollow, like I was doing it because I “should,” not because it came naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to be excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately nothing feels worth looking forward to. I still do them, but it’s like going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not soothing him right or I missed some cue. I know it’s probably not all on me, but the guilt just pops up before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll just be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet or his breathing sounds weird. I check the monitor a dozen times a night even when he’s fine. I know it’s probably nothing, but I can’t switch the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen to the baby or that I’ll completely mess up. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s awful while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me
Yes—most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby won’t settle, and I think, “I can’t do this.” I still manage, but it’s like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do I wake up at least once or twice panicking that I heard him cry or that he’s not breathing. I end up staring at the ceiling feeling completely drained.
I have felt sad or miserable
Pretty much every day. It’s like a heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be holding the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I just feel empty or like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week. Once was when the baby wouldn’t stop crying for almost an hour and I felt totally helpless; the other time was after a phone call with my mom—she asked how I was doing and I just burst into tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s crossed my mind, like a quick flash—what if I just weren’t here anymore—but then I picture the baby without me and I push it away. I haven’t made any plans or anything, but the thoughts have popped up once or twice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum EPDS-equivalent responses

Symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, emptiness (“heavy cloud,” daily sadness)
- Marked anhedonia (laughing feels hollow, no pleasure in previously enjoyed activities)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care
- Daily, intrusive anxious worries and nocturnal checking; repeated panic spells
- Overwhelm/demoralization (“drowning,” “can’t do this”)
- Sleep initiation/maintenance disturbance secondary to rumination
- Passive, transient self-harm thoughts (no plan, intent, or preparatory behavior)

Pattern: symptoms present most days for at least the past week, causing functional difficulty with infant care and self-care.

Screening significance:
- High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode plus comorbid anxiety symptoms
- Safety concern: presence of self-harm ideation warrants immediate risk assessment

Risk factors identified:
- Daily crying, pervasive anhedonia, guilt
- Sleep loss linked to mood
- Panic attacks and chronic worry
- Passive suicidal ideation (requires safety plan/clarification)

Next step: Recommend urgent clinical evaluation for formal diagnosis, safety planning, and discussion of treatment/support options.
